title: Kesh: hair as given
hookLine: uncut hair, kept as the Creator made it, and covered by the turban
last: REHAT — A WAY, NOT A LIST.

lines: ONE THING LEFT AS IT GREW.
cards: Haircuts, color, shaving, trimming, filters on every photo. So much of modern life is about changing how people look, and none of that is wrong.
Now imagine choosing, for your whole life, to leave one thing exactly as it grew. Not as a style. As a promise.
Millions of Sikhs do exactly that, and when you see a Sikh turban, you're seeing what it protects. Today, the first of the five articles of faith, the five Ks: kesh.

teach.b: Kesh means hair, and in Sikh practice it means uncut hair, kept whole from head to toe, as the Creator made it.

teach.h: THE FIRST OF THE FIVE KS, 1699.
teach.b: It's the first of the five Ks, the articles of faith that Sikh tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gave the Khalsa at Vaisakhi in 1699. All five begin with the sound k in Punjabi, which makes them easy to remember.
Why keep the hair? Sikhs give several reasons, and they fit together.
Acceptance: the body is the Creator's gift, and leaving it as made says, I accept the form I was given, in hukam, the order.
Identity: the Gurus themselves kept their hair, and keeping it says, I stand with them, where anyone can see. Discipline: it can't come off for the weekend.
A Sikh with uncut hair is recognizable on every street, and so accountable on every street.

In a hymn of Guru Arjan, in paraphrase, a true Muslim is described as keeping the whole form intact, with a turban on the head, and Sikhs often cite the phrase saabat soorat, the whole, intact form, as part of their own ideal.

The turban, the dastar, isn't one of the five Ks itself, but it protects and covers the kesh. Many Sikh men wear it, and some Sikh women do too; many more women cover their hair with a scarf, the chunni.
Not every Sikh keeps uncut hair: many honor the Gurus while cutting it, and the community talks about that openly. For those who keep it, the promise is simple.

how: Amritdhari Sikhs, and many other Sikhs, keep their hair uncut; many men and some women tie a turban (dastar) each day to cover it, while others cover it with a scarf (chunni).

games.q: a friend asks why a Sikh would keep uncut hair for life. which answer fits what you heard today?
o: it's accepting the body as the Creator made it, standing visibly with the Gurus, and a discipline you can't take off.
it's required of every person on earth.
games.why: acceptance, identity and discipline: kesh is kept as made, as a promise, not a style.

practice: If you can, move a brush, a comb or just your fingers slowly through your hair, as if it were a gift; if you have little or no hair, rest a hand gently on your head instead.
Notice the body you were given, its shape, its warmth, the way it grew without your planning. For a moment, don't improve anything; let it be as made.
